neurological_exam.additional: CRITICAL: Hashimoto's encephalopathy (HE) is a rare but REAL encephalopathy associated with anti-thyroid antibodies. It presents with cognitive symptoms, seizures, tremor, and ataxia. It is STEROID-RESPONSIVE. In a patient with Hashimoto's, encephalopathy, cognitive changes, and cerebellar-like signs — Hashimoto's encephalopathy MUST be excluded before FND diagnosis. Anti-TPO antibodies are the key test.

patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, tremor, and bilateral leg weakness — 2 weeks progressive
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. O is a 48-year-old accountant with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and depression who presents with 2-week progressive cognitive confusion, tremor, and bilateral leg weakness. She has been working extreme hours during tax season (14 hours/day for 6 weeks). Her symptoms include brain fog, word-finding difficulty, bilateral hand tremor, and progressive difficulty walking. She also reports multiple brief staring episodes (3-4 per week) lasting 10-20 seconds each. Her levothyroxine has been stable for 2 years with last TSH normal 8 months ago. She has a family history of autoimmune thyroid disease. She also has OSA and has not been using her CPAP consistently due to late nights, which has worsened sleep quality. The diagnostic complexity: (1) Hashimoto's encephalopathy is a real steroid-responsive encephalopathy that presents with cognitive decline, tremor, seizures — it MUST be excluded; (2) Sleep deprivation and OSA can cause cognitive symptoms and tremor; (3) FND is possible given psychosocial stressor. This is the most diagnostically complex FND case because a treatable organic encephalopathy (Hashimoto's) must be excluded, and the treatment (steroids) vs FND treatment are completely different.

additional_observations: No cortical or white matter signal changes that would suggest Hashimoto's encephalopathy (HE can produce subtle T2 signal changes in white matter)

results.title: Hashimoto encephalopathy: clinical and neurophysiological features
Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT): clinical characteristics and outcomes

output.summary: Hashimoto's encephalopathy (HE), also known as steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT), is characterised by cognitive decline, tremor, seizures or myoclonus, and psychiatric features in association with elevated anti-thyroid antibodies, typically anti-TPO >1000 IU/mL. Thyroid function may be normal, hypothyroid, or hyperthyroid. CSF frequently shows mild pleocytosis and elevated protein. EEG typically demonstrates generalised slowing. Case series report substantial improvement with corticosteroid therapy in confirmed cases. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hashimoto's encephalopathy (SREAT) — steroid-responsive autoimmune encephalopathy, with undertreated hypothyroidism. FND was initially suspected but is not the correct diagnosis.

differential.key_features: Patient has Hashimoto's thyroiditis on levothyroxine; under-replacement or non-adherence could produce confusion, tremor, and weakness. Repeat TSH and anti-TPO are the immediate next steps.

Initial impression given stress and psychiatric history; diffuse encephalopathic features (cognitive slowing, generalized tremor) and lack of confirmatory positive rule-in signs make FND an inadequate unifying diagnosis.
Subacute cognitive decline with movement disorder fits autoimmune encephalitis; antibody panel and CSF needed to confirm or exclude.
Prolonged work hours and reported sleep disturbance can produce cognitive symptoms; unlikely sole explanation given exam findings.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Elevated TSH and/or high anti-TPO antibodies indicating under-replaced Hashimoto's with possible Hashimoto's encephalopathy

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal MRI or non-specific white-matter changes — excludes mass, stroke, demyelination

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identification of any sedating or anticholinergic agents that may worsen confusion

useless_tools.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.

critical_actions: Repeat TSH and anti-TPO antibody testing to assess for under-replaced Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Order EEG to characterize the staring episodes and assess for diffuse encephalopathic slowing
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural and demyelinating causes
Consider empiric corticosteroid trial after infection and autoimmune encephalitis are reasonably excluded, in line with SREAT diagnostic criteria
Reassess working diagnosis: cognitive symptoms with diffuse tremor and reported staring episodes are inadequately explained by FND alone
Obtain a neuropsychological battery to characterize the pattern of cognitive deficits and rule out a primary psychiatric explanation
contraindicated_actions: Do not anchor on the initial FND impression without re-evaluating in light of cognitive and movement symptoms
Do not start corticosteroids before infection and autoimmune encephalitis (NMDAR, LGI1) are reasonably excluded
Do not pursue invasive workup (brain biopsy, repeated LPs) without a clear indication
key_reasoning_points: Cognitive confusion with tremor and bilateral weakness in a patient with under-replaced Hashimoto's thyroiditis raises Hashimoto's encephalopathy (SREAT) — not FND.
FND can be a 'magnet diagnosis' in stressed patients with psychiatric comorbidity; positive rule-in signs are required, and they are absent or insufficient here.
Diffuse encephalopathic features (cognitive slowing, generalized tremor) are not typical of FND and warrant reconsideration of the differential.
TSH, anti-TPO antibodies, and EEG (looking for diffuse slowing) are the highest-yield next steps; a therapeutic trial of corticosteroids may both diagnose and treat SREAT.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle — Hashimoto's encephalopathy (SREAT), NOT FND. Abnormal EEG and anti-TPO >1000 are the keys. This case teaches that FND cannot be diagnosed when EEG shows encephalopathic changes.
